## This tutorial
<blue>In this tutorial, we demonstrate forecasting the 2020Q1 CPI level, including stationarity tests, ARIMA model selection, and the final forecast computation.</blue>

<div style="height: 0.2em;"></div>
:::{.callout-note title = "Agenda"}

- <blue>Exercise 1(a):</blue> Transform CPI levels into log differences and select the ADF specification.

- <blue>Exercise 1(b):</blue> Test the log-differenced CPI for a unit root (ADF).

- <blue>Exercise 1(c):</blue> Select the ARIMA model using AICc and Ljung–Box diagnostics.

- <blue>Exercise 1(d):</blue> Does the choice of using observation indices or observation dates matter?

- <blue>Exercise 1(e):</blue> Forecast inflation and CPI for 2020Q1.


- <blue>Exercise 2:</blue> Rearranging a time series model into its corresponding ADF test equation.
:::

<div style="height: 0.2em;"></div>



## We know that taking the logs is not enough... {auto-animate="true"}
Recall the unit root test results for log `CPI` from Self-directed Activities 5.
```{r}
dt <- read.csv("CPI.csv")
Y <- ts(log(dt$CPI), start = c(1922,2), end = c(2025,2), frequency=4)
Y <- window(Y, start = c(1946,1), end = c(2019,4))
```

<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
```{r}
plot(Y)
```

An upward trend is obvious <blue>$\to$ add a time trend in deterministic specification<blue>

## We know that taking the logs is not enough... {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Carry out an ADF test of `Y`, present (i) the estimated test equation, 
(ii) the $t_{\text{ADF}}$ test statistic, 5\% critical value and decision, and (iii) its $p$-value.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

```{r}
library(urca)    # For use of ur.df function
adf <- ur.df(Y, type = "trend", selectlags = "AIC")
p_adf <- punitroot(adf@teststat[1], trend = "ct", statistic = "t")
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
::: {.panel-tabset}

## (i) test equation
The test equation is:
$$\Delta Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+\varphi Y_{t-1}+\sum^{p-1}_{k=1}\psi_{k} \Delta Y_{t-k}+U_{t}$$
The hypotheses are:
\begin{align}
H_{0}:&\;\varphi=0& &\textsf{($Y_{t}$ has a unit root)}\\
H_{1}:&\;\varphi<0& &\textsf{($Y_{t}$ does not have a unit root)}
\end{align}
The number of lags of $\Delta Y_{t}$ (i.e., $p-1$) is selected by an information criterion (AIC), where $p$ is the order of the underlying AR model.

## (ii) test summary
```{r}
summary(adf)
```

## (iii) $p$-value
```{r}
print(p_adf)
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
Since $p=0.997>0.05$, we <teal>**fail to reject** the null hypothesis $H_{0}$: there is unit root</teal>.
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

<blue>$\implies$ Simply removing the trend component is not enough to make $Y_{t}$ stationary. </blue>

<blue>$\implies$ We need to take the first difference of log `CPI`.</blue>
:::

## Exercise 1(a)
:::{.callout-question}
Next create the first difference time series $\Delta Y_{t}$ and a time series plot. Decide whether a trend is required for a unit root test for $\Delta Y_{t}$. 
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

```{r}
DY <- diff(Y)   # DY is the log difference of the CPI -> Inflation
plot(DY)
```
<blue>**Observation:** There is no evidence of a linear trend in this time series.</blue> There are some extended periods (e.g. early 1950's and 1970-80's) when inflation was higher.

## Exercise 1(b)  {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Carry out the unit root test on $\Delta Y_{t}$. Conclude how many differences are required for log CPI to be stationary.
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

```{r}
adf <- ur.df(DY, type = "drift", selectlags = "AIC")
p_adf <- punitroot(adf@teststat[1], trend = "c", statistic = "t")
summary(adf)
```
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
The estimated ADF test equation is:

$$\widehat{\Delta(\Delta Y_{t})}=0.0031-0.258\Delta Y_{t-1}-0.4253\Delta(\Delta Y_{t-1})$$

## Exercise 1(b)  {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Carry out the unit root test on $\Delta Y_{t}$. Conclude how many differences are required for log CPI to be stationary.
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

```{r}
adf <- ur.df(DY, type = "drift", selectlags = "AIC")
p_adf <- punitroot(adf@teststat[1], trend = "c", statistic = "t")
summary(adf)
```
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
The $t$-statistic is $-5.1529$, and the $5\%$ critical value is $-2.87$.

<blue>Since $-5.1539<-2.87$, we **reject** $H_0$: $\Delta Y_{t}$ has a unit root.</blue>


## Exercise 1(b)  {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Carry out the unit root test on $\Delta Y_{t}$. Conclude how many differences are required for log CPI to be stationary.
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

```{r eval=FALSE}
adf <- ur.df(DY, type = "drift", selectlags = "AIC")
p_adf <- punitroot(adf@teststat[1], trend = "c", statistic = "t")
summary(adf)
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

The $t$-statistic is $-5.1529$, and the $5\%$ critical value is $-2.87$.

Since $-5.1539<-2.87$, we **reject** $H_0$: $\Delta Y_{t}$ has a unit root.

::: {.fragment}
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
```{r}
print(p_adf)
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

:::


## Exercise 1(c)  {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Specify and estimate an appropriate ARIMA($p,d,q$) model for $Y_{t}$.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
:::{.callout-tip}
- Since first differencing is required for log CPI to be stationary, we need $d=1$.
- How to select $(p,q)$? <green>$\to$ Conduct a grid search for $p=0,\dots,4$ and $q=0,\dots,4$</green>
:::

<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
:::{.callout-note title="Code Structure"}
- Set up container matrices for AICc values (`AICc`) and Ljung-Box test $p$-values (`LBp`)

- For each $(p,q)$ combination:
  - Fit the ARIMA($p,1,q$) model with `Arima()` function, and extract AICc
  
  - Extract the Ljung-Box $p$-values with `checkresiduals()` function
  
- Choose the model with the **lowest** AICc, and verify that its <teal>Ljung-Box $H_{0}$ (no autocorrelation)</teal> is not rejected.

:::


## Exercise 1(c)  {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Specify and estimate an appropriate ARIMA($p,d,q$) model for $Y_{t}$.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
:::{.callout-tip}
- Since first differencing is required for log CPI to be stationary, we need $d=1$.
- How to select $(p,q)$? <green>$\to$ Conduct a grid search for $p=0,\dots,4$ and $q=0,\dots,4$</green>
:::


```{r}
library(forecast)

pmax <- 4
qmax <- 4

LBp <- matrix(nrow=pmax+1, ncol=qmax+1)
rownames(LBp) <- paste0("p=", 0:pmax)
colnames(LBp) <- paste0("q=", 0:qmax)
AICc <- LBp

for (p in 0:pmax){
  for (q in 0:qmax){
    eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(p,0,q))
    LBp[p+1,q+1] <- Box.test(eq$residuals, lag = 8, 
                             type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = p+q)$p.value
    AICc[p+1,q+1] <- eq$aicc
  }  
}
```


## Exercise 1(c)  {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Specify and estimate an appropriate ARIMA($p,d,q$) model for $Y_{t}$.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

Residual autocorrelation result (`=0` if $H_{0}$ maintained)
```{r}
print(LBp<0.05)
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

Model to minimise AICc:
```{r}
print(AICc==min(AICc))
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

:::{.fragment}

<blue>**Conclusion:** The chosen model is ARMA($1,3$) for $\Delta Y_{t}$, equivalently ARIMA($1,1,3$) for $Y_{t}$.</blue>
:::

## Exercise 1(c) {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
<blue>Model the linear trend using the observation indices $t=1,2,\dots,n$. </blue>

Combining a difference and a linear trend in the model requires some careful interpretation - write out the model in equation form and interpret the coefficients.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

:::{.panel-tabset}

## ARIMA(1,0,3) on $\Delta Y_{t}$

To estimate the ARIMA(1,0,3) model for $\Delta Y_{t}$, with that difference already taken in computing `DY`:
```{r}
eq_a <- Arima(DY, order = c(1,0,3))
print(round(eq_a$coef,4))
```
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
In equation form, this estimated model can be written as:

\begin{align}
\Delta Y_{t}&=0.0120 +\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t}\\
\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t}&=0.8316\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t-1}+\widehat{U}_{t}-0.6377\widehat{U}_{t-1}+0.2380\widehat{U}_{t-2}+0.1276\widehat{U}_{t-3}
\end{align}

The intercept of the model, $\widehat{\beta}_{1}=0.0120$, implies the estimated mean rate of inflation is $0.0120$, or $1.2\%$ per quarter (this is a qurterly time series).

## ARIMA(1,1,3) on $Y_{t}$
The same model may be estimated as an ARIMA($1,1,3$) model for $Y_{t}$:
```{r}
eq_b <- Arima(Y, order = c(1,1,3), include.drift = TRUE)
print(round(eq_b$coef,4))
```
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>

\begin{align}
 Y_{t}&=0.0120t +\widehat{Z}_{t}\\
\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t}&=0.8316\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t-1}+\widehat{U}_{t}-0.6377\widehat{U}_{t-1}+0.2380\widehat{U}_{t-2}+0.1276\widehat{U}_{t-3}
\end{align}

:::{.callout-note title = "Note"}
- `include.drift = TRUE` option is necessary for the inclusion of $\beta_{1}$ when the differencing is specified under `order = c(1,1,3)` rather than taking the difference beforehand and included in the model as `DY`.
- It is called "drift" because a constant in a first-differenced process corresponds to a linear trend in the level of $Y_{t}$.
- Alternatively, replicating this with `xreg` argument:
```{r}
t <- 1:length(Y)
eq_b_xreg <- Arima(Y, order = c(1,1,3), xreg = t)
print(round(eq_b_xreg$coef,4))
```
:::



## Comments on Forecasting
```{r}
print(round(eq_a$coef,4))
print(round(eq_b$coef,4))
```
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
- The two approaches are equivalent for estimation, as can be seen from these coefficient estimates. There is a difference, however, between the two when it comes to forecasting. 
  - The ARMA(1,3) model on $\Delta Y_{t}$ (`DY`) will generate forecasts for $\Delta Y_{t}$ (inflation), while the second is model for $Y_{t}$ (`Y`, log CPI). <blue>$\to$ We will demonstrate this in part (e).</blue>
- Neither is necessarily better/worse, it just depends on the intended purpose.

:::

## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
In previous applications we have modeled the linear trend using the observation *dates* $\text{Time}_{t}$. Set up the same ARIMA$(p,d,q)$ model for $Y_{t}$ as (c), but use the observation dates instead. 

<blue>Show how this is equivalent to using observation indices for the trend.</blue>
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
We start from the trend model with observation *indices* ($t$):
\begin{align}
Y_{t}&=\mathbb{E}(Y_{t})+Z_{t}\\
\textsf{where}\quad \mathbb{E}(Y_{t})&=\beta_{0}+\textcolor{black}{\beta_{1}}t & &\textsf{(Trend model with observation indices)}\\
\mathbb{E}(Y_{t})&=\beta^{*}_{0}+\beta^{*}_{1}\text{Time}_{t} & &\textsf{(Trend model with observation dates)}
\end{align}

## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
In previous applications we have modeled the linear trend using the observation *dates* $\text{Time}_{t}$. Set up the same ARIMA$(p,d,q)$ model for $Y_{t}$ as (c), but use the observation dates instead. 

<blue>Show how this is equivalent to using observation indices for the trend.</blue>
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
We start from the trend model with observation *indices* ($t$):
\begin{align}
Y_{t}&=\mathbb{E}(Y_{t})+Z_{t}\\
\textsf{where}\quad \mathbb{E}(Y_{t})&=\beta_{0}+\textcolor{purple}{\beta_{1}}t & &\textsf{(Trend model with observation indices)}\\
\mathbb{E}(Y_{t})&=\beta^{*}_{0}+\beta^{*}_{1}\text{Time}_{t} & &\textsf{(Trend model with observation dates)}
\end{align}

<purple>The interpretation of $\beta_{1}$ is the change in mean of $Y_{t}$ when $t$ increases by one (i.e. when time advances by one period, one *quarter* in this case.)</purple>

In previous applications we have modeled the linear trend using the observation *dates* $\text{Time}_{t}$. Set up the same ARIMA$(p,d,q)$ model for $Y_{t}$ as (c), but use the observation dates instead.

:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
We start from the trend model with observation *indices* ($t$):

<purple>The interpretation of $\beta_{1}$ is the change in mean of $Y_{t}$ when $t$ increases by one (i.e. when time advances by one period, one *quarter* in this case.)</purple>

<teal>The interpretation of $\beta^{*}_{1}$ is the change in mean of $Y_{t}$ when $\text{Time}_{t}$ increases by one (i.e. one *year* in this case.)</teal>

<div style="height: 0.2em;"></div>
:::{.fragment}
<blue>**Question:** </blue>How are $\textcolor{purple}{\beta_{1}}$ and $\textcolor{teal}{\beta^{*}_{1}}$ related?

## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
In previous applications we have modeled the linear trend using the observation *dates* $\text{Time}_{t}$. Set up the same ARIMA$(p,d,q)$ model for $Y_{t}$ as (c), but use the observation dates instead. 

<blue>Show how this is equivalent to using observation indices for the trend.</blue>
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
We start from the trend model with observation *indices* ($t$):
\begin{align}
Y_{t}&=\mathbb{E}(Y_{t})+Z_{t}\\
\textsf{where}\quad \mathbb{E}(Y_{t})&=\beta_{0}+\textcolor{purple}{\beta_{1}}t & &\textsf{(Trend model with observation indices)}\\
\mathbb{E}(Y_{t})&=\beta^{*}_{0}+\textcolor{teal}{\beta^{*}_{1}}\text{Time}_{t} & &\textsf{(Trend model with observation dates)}
\end{align}

<blue>**Question:** </blue>How are $\textcolor{purple}{\beta_{1}}$ and $\textcolor{teal}{\beta^{*}_{1}}$ related? [<green>$\to$ Intuitively, with quarterly data $\beta_{1}=0.25\beta^{*}_{1}$.</green>]{.fragment}

:::{.incremental}

- We start with $\textcolor{teal}{\text{Time}_{t}=1945.75+0.25t}$.
- Then plugging this into the trend model with observation dates:
\begin{align}
Y_{t}&=\beta_{0}^*+\beta_{1}^{*}\textcolor{teal}{\text{Time}_{t}}+Z_{t}\\
&=\beta_{0}^*+\beta_{1}^{*}(\textcolor{teal}{1945.75+0.25t})+Z_{t}\\
&=\textcolor{purple}{(\beta_{0}^{*}+1945.75\beta_{1}^*)}+\textcolor{purple}{0.25\beta_{1}^{*}}t+Z_{t}
\end{align}
- Reading off the coefficients, we know <purple>$\beta_{0}=\beta_{0}^{*}+1045.75\beta_{1}^{*}$</purple> and <purple>$\beta_{1}=0.25\beta_{1}^*$</purple>.
:::



## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
In previous applications we have modeled the linear trend using the observation *dates* $\text{Time}_{t}$. Set up the same ARIMA$(p,d,q)$ model for $Y_{t}$ as (c), but use the observation dates instead. 

<blue>Show how this is equivalent to using observation indices for the trend.</blue>
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
```{r}
t <- 1:length(Y)
eq_b <- Arima(Y, order = c(1,1,3), include.drift = TRUE) 
# Equivalently eq_b_xreg <- Arima(Y, order = c(1,1,3), xreg = t)  
print(round(eq_b$coef,4))
```
::: {style="position: absolute; left: 39%; top: 42%; width: 110px; height: 70px; border: 3px solid purple; background: transparent; box-sizing: border-box;"}
:::
::: {style="position: absolute; left: 48.5%; top: 42%; width: 110px; height: 70px; border: 0px solid teal; background: transparent; box-sizing: border-box;"}
<purple>$\beta_{1}$</purple>
:::

:::{.fragment}
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
```{r}
Time <- time(Y)
# include.drift = FALSE is actually the default, but it is included here to 
# emphasise the point
eq_c <- Arima(Y, order = c(1,1,3), xreg = Time, include.drift = FALSE)
print(round(eq_c$coef,4))
```
::: {style="position: absolute; left: 39%; top: 71%; width: 110px; height: 70px; border: 3px solid teal; background: transparent; box-sizing: border-box;"}
:::
::: {style="position: absolute; left: 48.5%; top: 71%; width: 110px; height: 70px; border: 0px solid teal; background: transparent; box-sizing: border-box;"}
<teal>$\beta_{1}^*$</teal>
:::
:::

:::{.fragment}
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
```{r}
print(eq_c$coef["xreg"]/eq_b$coef["drift"])   # beta1*/beta1
```
::: {style="position: absolute; left: 15%; top: 86%; width: 110px; height: 70px; border: 0px solid teal; background: transparent; box-sizing: border-box;"}
$\textcolor{teal}{\beta_{1}^*}/\textcolor{purple}{\beta_{1}}$
:::
:::

:::{.fragment}
<blue>**Bottom Line: **We may model the linear trend in terms of observation date or observation index, according to which is more convenient, and the resulting model will be equivalent either way.</blue>
:::


## Exercise 1(e)  {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of <blue>inflation</blue>, $\log(CPI_{t})$ and the $CPI_{t}$ itself for the March quarter of 2020.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
:::{.callout-tip}
Note that we have selected ARMA(1,3) for $\Delta Y_{t}\equiv \Delta\log(CPI_{t})$ in Exercise 1(c).
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

:::{.fragment}
Forecast 2020Q1 inflation:  $\Delta{}Y_{2020Q1}=\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})$
```{r}
# Recall: eq_a <- Arima(DY, order = c(1,0,3))
ForecastInflation_2020q1 <- forecast(eq_a, h=1)$mean
print(round(ForecastInflation_2020q1, 4))
```
:::

:::{.fragment}
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
**The inflation forecast is based on an approximation…**

Recall from Week 1 tutorial that for small $r$ values, $\log(1+r)\approx r$:
\begin{align}
CPI_{2019Q4}(1+\text{inflation}_{2020Q1})&=CPI_{2020Q1}\\
\log(1+\text{inflation}_{2020Q1})&=\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})\\
\implies\qquad \color{blue}{\text{inflation}_{2020Q1}}&\approx\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})
\end{align}
:::

Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation, <blue>$\log(CPI_{t})$</blue> and the $CPI_{t}$ itself for the March quarter of 2020.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
:::{.callout-tip}
Note that we have selected ARMA(1,3) for $\Delta Y_{t}\equiv \Delta\log(CPI_{t})$ in Exercise 1(c).
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

Forecast 2020Q1 inflation:  $\Delta{}Y_{2020Q1}=\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})$
```{r echo=FALSE}
# Recall: eq_a <- Arima(DY, order = c(1,0,3))
ForecastInflation_2020q1 <- forecast(eq_a, h=1)$mean
print(round(ForecastInflation_2020q1, 4))
```
::: {style="position: absolute; left: 20%; top: 40%; width: 110px; height: 70px; border: 0px solid teal; background: transparent; box-sizing: border-box;"}
<purple>$\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\Delta Y_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n})$</purple>
:::
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
Forecast 2020Q1 $\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\equiv Y_{2020Q1}$:

:::{.incremental}
- First we know that $\Delta Y_{2020Q1}=Y_{2020Q1}-Y_{2019Q4}$.
- On both sides take the conditional expectation based on data up to and including 2019Q4 ($\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4}$):
$$\mathbb{E}(\Delta Y_{2020Q1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4})=\mathbb{E}(Y_{2020Q1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4})-\mathbb{E}(Y_{2019Q4}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4})$$
- Since $Y_{2019Q4}\in\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4}$, $\mathbb{E}(Y_{2019Q4}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4})=Y_{2019Q4}$, thus adding hats gives:
$$\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y_{2020Q1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4})=Y_{2019Q4}+\textcolor{purple}{\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\Delta Y_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n})}$$
:::

## Exercise 1(e)  {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation, $\log(CPI_{t})$ and the <blue>$CPI_{t}$ itself</blue> for the March quarter of 2020.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
**Remarks on the CPI forecasts:** 

Both approaches are approximations.


<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})$


<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\color{blue}{\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4}]}\color{black}{)}$
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
<oblue>
**Question:** Does the following hold?
$$\color{blue}{\mathbb{E}[{CPI}_{2020Q1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4}]\overset{?}{=}\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4}])}$$
</oblue>


:::{.fragment}
<blue>
**Answer:** No. This is because of Jensen's inequality - since $\exp(x)$ is convex:
$$\mathbb{E}[\exp(\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4})]>\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4}])$$
</blue>
:::


## Exercise 1(e)  {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation, $\log(CPI_{t})$ and the <blue>$CPI_{t}$ itself</blue> for the March quarter of 2020.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
**Remarks on the CPI forecasts:** 

Both approaches are approximations.


<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})$


<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4}]\color{black}{)}$
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
<blue>
Thus this estimator is actually biased for the conditional mean  $\mathbb{E}[CPI_{2020Q1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4}]$:
$$\mathbb{E}[CPI_{2020Q1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4}]>\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathscr{Y}_{2019Q4}])$$
</blue>

:::{.fragment}
<green>
Nevertheless, in practice and [by research](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169207011000112), simply taking the exponential tends to work well in providing a good approximation. 
So we will continue to take exponentials whenever required.
</green>
:::



## Exercise 2 {auto-animate="true"}
Consider a time series model consisting of a trend equation and AR(p) equation:
\begin{align}
Y_{t}&=X_{t}^{\top}\beta +Z_{t}\\
Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}+\cdots+\phi_{p}Z_{t-p}+U_{t}
\end{align}



:::{.fragment}
<purple>
The ADF equation for this model is:
$$\Delta Y_{t}=\varphi Y_{t-1}+X_{t}^{\top}\beta^{*}+\sum^{p-1}_{k=1}\psi_{k}\Delta Y_{t-k}+U_{t}$$
</purple>
i.e. a regression of $\Delta Y_{t}$ on

- $Y_{t-1}$: variable of interest for the ADF test;
- $X_{t}$: same set of deterministic variables as specified in the original model
- lags $1,\dots,p-1$ of $\Delta Y_{t}$ (i.e. one fewer lag than in the original model).

Note the coefficients on $X_{t}$ in the original model ($\beta$) differ from those in the ADF test equation ($\beta^*$).
:::


## Exercise 2 {auto-animate="true"}
Consider a time series model consisting of a trend equation and AR(p) equation:
\begin{align}
Y_{t}&=X_{t}^{\top}\beta +Z_{t}\\
Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}+\cdots+\phi_{p}Z_{t-p}+U_{t}
\end{align}

<purple>
The ADF equation for this model is:
$$\Delta Y_{t}=\varphi Y_{t-1}+X_{t}^{\top}\beta^{*}+\sum^{p-1}_{k=1}\psi_{k}\Delta Y_{t-k}+U_{t}$$
</purple>

Note the coefficients on $X_{t}$ in the original model ($\beta$) differ from those in the ADF test equation ($\beta^*$). [<teal>$\to$ How are these coefficients related?</teal>]{.fragment}
<div style="height: 1em;"></div>

:::{.fragment}

:::{.callout-question}
Let's work through an example of how a specific time series model can be rearranged into the ADF equation. Consider a model with intercept and linear trend, and 2 lags in the AR equation:
\begin{align}
Y_{t}&=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1} t+Z_{t}\\
Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}+\phi_{2}Z_{t-2}+U_{t}
\end{align}
<blue>
Goal: Rewrite these equations in the form of the ADF equation, derive $\beta_{0}^{*}$ and $\beta_{1}^{*}$:
$$\Delta Y_{t}=\varphi Y_{t-1}+\beta_{0}^{*}+\beta_{1}^{*}t+\psi_{1}\Delta Y_{t-1}+U_{t}$$
</blue>
:::
:::



## Exercise 2 {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Consider a model with intercept and linear trend, and 2 lags in the AR equation:
\begin{align}
Y_{t}&=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1} t+Z_{t}\\
Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}+\phi_{2}Z_{t-2}+U_{t}
\end{align}
<blue>
Goal: Rewrite these equations in the form of the ADF equation, derive $\beta_{0}^{*}$ and $\beta_{1}^{*}$:
$$\Delta Y_{t}=\varphi Y_{t-1}+\beta_{0}^{*}+\beta_{1}^{*}t+\psi_{1}\Delta Y_{t-1}+U_{t}$$
</blue>
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
 
:::{.panel-tabset}
## Step 1
Re-express the autoregressive equation in the form
$$\Delta Z_{t}=\varphi Z_{t-1}+\psi_{1}\Delta Z_{t-1}+U_{t}$$
where $\varphi = \phi_{1}+\phi_{2}-1$ and $\psi_{1}=-\phi_{2}$.
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>

\begin{align}
Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}+\phi_{2}Z_{t-2}+U_{t}\\
Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}\textcolor{magenta}{+\phi_{2}Z_{t-1}-\phi_{2}Z_{t-1}}+\phi_{2}Z_{t-2}+U_{t}\\
Z_{t}&=\textcolor{blue}{(\phi_{1}+\phi_{2})Z_{t-1}}\textcolor{green}{-\phi_{2}\Delta Z_{t-1}}+U_{t}\\
Z_{t}\textcolor{red}{-Z_{t-1}}&=\textcolor{red}{-Z_{t-1}}+(\phi_{1}+\phi_{2})Z_{t-1}-\phi_{2}\Delta Z_{t-1}+U_{t}\\
\Delta Z_{t}&=\varphi Z_{t-1}+\psi_{1}\Delta Z_{t-1}+U_{t}

\end{align}
where $\varphi=\phi_{1}+\phi_{2}-1$ and $\psi_{1}=-\phi_{2}$.

## Step 2
From Step 1 we have 
$$\textcolor{red}{\Delta Z_{t}}=\varphi \textcolor{blue}{Z_{t-1}}+\psi_{1}\textcolor{magenta}{\Delta Z_{t-1}}+U_{t}.$$
Using the trend equation $Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}$, derive the following:
\begin{align}
\textcolor{red}{\Delta Z_{t}}\;&\textcolor{red}{=\Delta Y_{t}-\beta_{1}}\\
\textcolor{magenta}{\Delta Z_{t-1}}\;&\textcolor{magenta}{=\Delta Y_{t-1}-\beta_{1}}\\
\textcolor{blue}{Z_{t-1}}\;&\textcolor{blue}{=Y_{t-1}-\beta_{0}-\beta_{1}(t-1)}
\end{align}
substituting gives $(\textcolor{red}{\Delta Y_{t}-\beta_{1}})=\varphi(\textcolor{blue}{Y_{t-1}-\beta_{0}-\beta_{1}(t-1)})+\psi_{1}(\textcolor{magenta}{\Delta Y_{t-1}-\beta_{1}})+U_{t}$

## Step 2 Derivations

- Starting from the trend equation $Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}$, the first lag is:
\begin{align}
Y_{t-1}&=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}(t-1)+Z_{t-1}\quad\quad\quad (1)\\
\implies \textcolor{blue}{Z_{t-1}}\;&\textcolor{blue}{=Y_{t-1}-\beta_{0}-\beta_{1}(t-1)}
\end{align}
- Using equation (1) and the trend equation, we thus know that:
\begin{align}
&&Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}&=(\beta_{0}-\beta_{0})+\beta_{1}(t-(t-1))+Z_{t}-Z_{t-1}\\
&&\Delta Y_{t}&=\beta_{1}+\Delta {Z_{t}}\\
\implies&& \textcolor{red}{\Delta Z_{t}}\;&\textcolor{red}{=\Delta Y_{t}-\beta_{1}}\\
\implies&& \textcolor{magenta}{\Delta Z_{t-1}}\;&\textcolor{magenta}{=\Delta Y_{t-1}-\beta_{1}}
\end{align}


## Step 3
From Step 2 we have:
$$(\textcolor{red}{\Delta Y_{t}-\beta_{1}})=\varphi(\textcolor{blue}{Y_{t-1}-\beta_{0}-\beta_{1}(t-1)})+\psi_{1}(\textcolor{magenta}{\Delta Y_{t-1}-\beta_{1}})+U_{t}$$
Simplify this to the form of ADF test equation: 
$$\Delta Y_{t}=\varphi Y_{t-1}+\textcolor{green}{\beta_{0}^{*}}+\textcolor{teal}{\beta_{1}^{*}}t+\psi_{1}\Delta Y_{t-1}+U_{t}$$
where $\textcolor{green}{\beta_{0}^{*}=\beta_{1}-\varphi\beta_{0}+\varphi\beta_{1}-\psi_{1}\beta_{1}}$ and $\textcolor{teal}{\beta_{1}^{*}=-\varphi\beta_{1}}$.

## Step 3 Algebra
\begin{align}
(\Delta Y_{t}-\beta_{1})&=\varphi(Y_{t-1}-\beta_{0}-\beta_{1}(t-1))+\psi_{1}(\Delta Y_{t-1}-\beta_{1})+U_{t}\\
\Delta Y_{t}&=\beta_{1}+\varphi Y_{t-1}-\varphi\beta_{0}-\varphi\beta_{1} t+\varphi\beta_{1}+\psi_{1}\Delta Y_{t-1}-\psi_{1}\beta_{1}+U_{t}\\
\Delta Y_{t}&=\varphi Y_{t-1}+\beta_{1}-\varphi\beta_{0}+\varphi\beta_{1}-\psi_{1}\beta_{1}-\varphi\beta_{1}t+\psi_{1}\Delta Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\\
\Delta Y_{t}&=\varphi Y_{t-1}+\textcolor{green}{\underbrace{(\beta_{1}-\varphi\beta_{0}+\varphi\beta_{1}-\psi_{1}\beta_{1})}_{\equiv\beta_{0}^{*}}}+\textcolor{teal}{\underbrace{(-\varphi\beta_{1})}_{\equiv\beta_{1}^{*}}}t+\psi_{1}\Delta Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\\
\Delta Y_{t}&=\varphi Y_{t-1}+\textcolor{green}{\beta_{0}^{*}}+\textcolor{teal}{\beta_{1}^{*}}t+\psi_{1}\Delta Y_{t-1}+U_{t}
\end{align}
where $\textcolor{green}{\beta_{0}^{*}=\beta_{1}-\varphi\beta_{0}+\varphi\beta_{1}-\psi_{1}\beta_{1}}$ and $\textcolor{teal}{\beta_{1}^{*}=-\varphi\beta_{1}}$.

## Discussion
- This derivation is intended to show how the ADF test equation follows from a time series model, including:
  - how the lag length is reduced by one, and
  - how the deterministic coefficients differ between the trend equation and ADF test equation.

- Having seen this once, the details become practically unimportant thereafter.
  - The values of the deterministic coefficients in the ADF test regression are not directly interesting in themselves.

- The important thing is the specification of an appropriate ADF test equation from a time series model if it has already been specified.

:::
